# 4.6 – Graphing Linear Inequalities {.unnumbered}

You’ve learned how to **graph lines** from equations like $y = 2x + 3$.
Now we’ll take that same idea and add one new twist — an **inequality symbol**.

When we switch from **equations** to **inequalities**, we’re no longer looking for one line that fits. We’re looking for **all the points that make the inequality true** — a whole region of the graph.

:::{.objectives}

* [ ] I can graph linear inequalities in two variables.
* [ ] I can solve linear inequalities in two variables and graph the solution.
* [ ] I can solve systems of linear inequalities.

:::

:::{.vocab}
{{< glink inequality >}}, {{< glink greater than >}}, {{< glink less than >}}, {{< glink dashed line >}}, {{< glink solid line >}}, {{< glink solution set >}}
:::

{{< warmup >}}

1. Solve for $x$: $4x - 7 < 13$

2. Solve for $y$: $-3y + 6 \ge 9$

3. Graph the line $y = -\tfrac{2}{3}x + 1$.

{{< learn >}}

### 4.6.1 – Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

Back in Unit 3, you learned that solving an **inequality** is almost the same as solving an **equation**, with just a few key differences:

* If you multiply or divide by a negative number, you **flip the inequality sign**.
* The solution is not a single number but a **range of values**.
* The difference between $x > 5$ and $x \ge 5$ is whether the endpoint is **included** (closed circle) or **not included** (open circle).

Those same ideas still apply when we move to **two variables**, but now our solutions appear on a **coordinate plane** instead of a number line.

---

Let’s start with what you already know.

When you graph $x > 5$, you use an **open circle** at 5 and shade to the right:

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/xgt5.png){width="500px" fig-align="center"}

If the inequality is $x \ge 5$, you use a **closed circle** at 5 and again shade to the right:

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/xgte5.png){width="500px" fig-align="center"}

---

Now we’ll extend those ideas to the coordinate plane.

| On a number line                  | On a coordinate plane                                |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Open circle → point not included  | **Dashed line** → points on the line not included    |
| Closed circle → point included    | **Solid line** → points on the line included         |
| Arrow to the right → greater than | **Shade above** the line → greater than ($>$ or $≥$) |
| Arrow to the left → less than     | **Shade below** the line → less than ($<$ or $≤$)    |

---

**Example 1**
Graph the inequality $y \le \tfrac{1}{2}x + 2$.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example1.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

The shaded region shows all points **below** the line.
The line is **solid**, so points on the line are **included** in the solution set.

We can use a **test point** to confirm.

The point $(-4, 6)$ appears **outside** the shaded region:
$$
\begin{align*}
6 &\le \tfrac{1}{2}(-4) + 2 \\
6 &\le 0
\end{align*}
$$
This is **false**, so $(-4, 6)$ is correctly outside the solution.

The point $(2, -4)$ appears **inside** the shaded region:
$$
\begin{align*}
-4 &\le \tfrac{1}{2}(2) + 2 \\
-4 &\le 3
\end{align*}
$$
This is **true**, confirming that $(2, -4)$ is part of the solution set.

---

**Example 2**
Graph the inequality $y < \tfrac{1}{2}x + 2$.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example2.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

The shaded region shows all points **below** the line.
The line is **dashed**, so points on the line are **not included**.

---

**Example 3**
Graph the inequality $y > \tfrac{1}{2}x + 2$.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example3.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

The shaded region shows all points **above** the line.
The line is **dashed**, so points on the line are **not included**.

---

**Example 4**
Graph the inequality $y \ge \tfrac{1}{2}x + 2$.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example4.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

The shaded region shows all points **above** the line.
The line is **solid**, so points on the line are **included**.

:::{.you-try title="Graph the inequality $y < 3x - 5$"}
![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/YouTry1.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}
:::

---

### 4.6.2 – Solving Two-Variable Inequalities

In the last section, you graphed a linear inequality once it was already written as $y < mx + b$ or $y \le mx + b$.

But what if $y$ isn’t by itself yet?
Here we’ll focus on **getting the inequality into slope-intercept form** so it’s ready to graph.

---

**How to solve for $y$:**

1. Move $x$-terms and constants just like in an equation.
2. If you multiply or divide by a **negative**, **flip the inequality sign**.
3. Once it’s in slope-intercept form ($y = mx + b$), graph it as before:

   * **Dashed line** for $<$ or $>$
   * **Solid line** for $\le$ or $\ge$
   * **Shade above** for “greater,” **below** for “less”

---

**Example 1**

Solve and graph $2x + y < 4$.
$$
\begin{align*}
2x + y &< 4 \\
y &< -2x + 4
\end{align*}
$$
The line $y = -2x + 4$ is **dashed** and shaded **below**.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example5.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

---

**Example 2**

Solve and graph $3x - 2y \le 6$.
$$
\begin{align*}
3x - 2y &\le 6 \\
-2y &\le -3x + 6 \\
y &\ge \tfrac{3}{2}x - 3 \quad \text{(flip the sign when dividing by –2)}
\end{align*}
$$
The line $y = \tfrac{3}{2}x - 3$ is **solid** and shaded **above**.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example6.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.gotcha title="Don’t forget to flip the sign!"}
When you multiply or divide both sides by a **negative number**, the inequality **reverses direction**.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Solve and graph 4x - 2y ≤ 8"}
$$
y \ge 2x - 4
$$

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/YouTry2.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}
:::

---

### 4.6.3 – Systems of Linear Inequalities

So far, you’ve graphed a **single inequality** — one shaded region showing all the points that make it true.

A **system of inequalities** means you have **two or more inequalities** on the same graph.
Each one creates its own shaded region.
The **solution set** is where all the shaded regions **overlap**.

That overlapping area shows all the $(x, y)$ pairs that make **every inequality true** at the same time.

---

**Example 7**

Graph the system:
$$
\begin{aligned}
y &\le 2x + 3 \\
y &> -x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Steps:

1. Graph $y = 2x + 3$ with a **solid line** and shade **below** it.
2. Graph $y = -x + 1$ with a **dashed line** and shade **above** it.
3. The **overlapping region** (where both shades meet) is the **solution set**.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example7.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

Any point in that shaded overlap makes both inequalities true.
For example, $(4, 2)$ works because:
$$
\begin{aligned}
2 &\le 2(4) + 3 = 11 \quad \text{(true)} \\
2 &> -4 + 1 = -3 \quad \text{(true)}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

**Example 8**

Some systems create a **closed shape** when the shaded areas overlap.
These are common in real-world problems with limits or constraints.
$$
\begin{aligned}
y &\le -x + 5 \\
y &\le x + 1 \\
y &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Steps:

1. Graph each line (the top two are solid and shade **below**; the last shades **above** the $x$-axis).
2. The shaded **triangle** that forms where all three regions meet is the **solution**.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/Example8.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}

Any point inside that triangle satisfies **all three inequalities**.

---

:::{.you-try-m title="Graph and describe the solution region."}
$$
\begin{aligned}
y &> -x + 2 \\
y &< 3x + 6
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

:::{.answer title="Answer"}
![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_6/YouTry3.png){width="450px" fig-align="center"}
:::

:::{.remember title="What the overlap means"}
Each shaded region shows where **one inequality** is true.
The **overlap** shows where **all inequalities** are true together — the solution set.

In real-world problems, this region represents all combinations that **meet every condition** (for example, time, budget, or resource limits).
:::

{{< practice >}}

1. For $y \le -3x + 2$: say whether the boundary is **solid or dashed**, and whether you shade **above or below**.

2. For $y > \tfrac{1}{2}x - 4$: boundary type and shading direction?

3. Rewrite in slope-intercept form and state $(m, b)$:
   $3x + y \ge 5$.

4. Rewrite and state boundary/shading:
   $-2y < 6x - 8$.

5. Test whether the point is a solution to $y \le x + 1$: $(2, 3)$.

6. Test whether the point is a solution to $y \le x + 1$: $(0, 2)$.

7. **Graphing (describe):** For $y < -x$, draw the boundary and describe which side to shade.

8. A boundary line passes through $(0, -2)$ and $(2, 2)$. The region is **above** the boundary and the boundary is **not included**. Write an inequality in the form $y \ \square\  mx + b$.

9. For the system

   $$
    \begin{align*}
    y &>= -x + 1 \\
    y &< 2x + 5
    \end{align*}
   $$

   is $(2, 4)$ a solution?

10. For the system
    $$
    \begin{align*}
    y &\le 3 - x \\
    y &\ge -2
    \end{align*}
    $$

    is $(5, -1)$ a solution?

11. Put $4x - 2y \ge 8$ into slope-intercept form and state boundary/shading.

12. **Graphing (describe):** Draw the dashed line $y = -\tfrac{1}{2}x + 4$ and indicate which side to shade for $y < -\tfrac{1}{2}x + 4$.

13. For the system
    $$
    \begin{align*}
    y &\ge 0 \\
    x &\ge 0 \\
    y &\le -x + 6
    \end{align*}
    $$

    list the **vertices** of the triangular solution region.

14. The boundary is $y = \tfrac{1}{3}x + 1$, the region is **above**, and the boundary **is included**. Write the inequality.

15. Without rearranging, decide boundary/shading for $y > 2 - \tfrac{3}{4}x$.

16. Solve for $y$, then say whether the origin $(0,0)$ lies in the solution:
    $-x + 3y > 9$.

17. True/False: “If a point lies on the boundary of $y < 2x + 1$, then it is part of the solution set.”

18. For the pair of inequalities $y \ge x - 1$ and $y \le x + 2$:
    a) Describe the shape of the solution region.
    b) Is $(0,0)$ in the solution?

19. An open boundary through $(-2, 1)$ and $(2, -1)$ with the region **below** the line. Write the inequality.

20. Determine if the system has **any** solutions (yes/no). Briefly justify.
    $$
    \begin{align*}
    y &< x - 5 \\
    y &> x + 1
    \end{align*}
    $$

21. Write an inequality whose solution is “all points with $y$ at least $-2$”. State boundary/shading.

22. Shade “to the right of” the vertical line $x = -3$, boundary **not included**. Write the inequality.

23. **Graphing (describe):** For the system
    $$
    \begin{align*}
    y &\le 2x + 1 \\
    y &\ge -x - 2
    \end{align*}
    $$

    describe the overlap and decide if $(3,0)$ is included.

24. **Challenge.** For the system
    
    $$
    \begin{align*}
    y &\ge x - 1 \\
    y &\ge -x - 1 \\
    y &\le 4
    \end{align*}
    $$

    find the **vertices** of the (bounded) solution region.

25. **Challenge.** A triangular region has vertices $(0,0),\ (4,0),\ (1,3)$. Write a system of **three** linear inequalities (with $\le$ or $\ge$) whose solution set is exactly this triangle (including edges).

---

:::{.answers}

1. **Solid**, shade **below** (because (\le)).
2. **Dashed**, shade **above** (because (>)).
3. (y \ge -3x + 5). So (m=-3,\ b=5); **solid**, shade **above**.
4. Divide by (-2) (flip): (y > -3x + 4). **Dashed**, shade **above**.
5. Check (3 \le 2 + 1\Rightarrow 3 \le 3) **true** → solution.
6. Check (2 \le 0 + 1\Rightarrow 2 \le 1) **false** → not a solution.
7. Boundary: line (y = -x), **dashed**; shade **below** the line.
8. Slope (m=\dfrac{2-(-2)}{2-0}=2), intercept (b=-2) ⇒ line (y=2x-2). Above & not included ⇒ (\boxed{,y > 2x - 2,}).
9. ((2,4)): (4 \ge -2 + 1=-1) true; (4 < 9) true ⇒ **yes**.
10. ((5,-1)): (-1 \le 3-5=-2) **false** ⇒ **no**.
11. (4x - 2y \ge 8 \Rightarrow -2y \ge 8 - 4x \Rightarrow y \le 2x - 4). **Solid**, shade **below**.
12. For (y < -\tfrac{1}{2}x + 4): draw **dashed** (y=-\tfrac{1}{2}x+4), shade **below**.
13. First-quadrant triangle under (y=-x+6): vertices (\boxed{(0,0),\ (6,0),\ (0,6)}).
14. Above and included ⇒ (\boxed{,y \ge \tfrac{1}{3}x + 1,}).
15. Already in (y > \cdots) form: **dashed**, shade **above**.
16. (-x + 3y > 9 \Rightarrow 3y > x + 9 \Rightarrow y > \tfrac{1}{3}x + 3).
    Test origin: (0 > 3) **false**, so the side **not** containing ((0,0)).
17. **False.** Strict inequality (<) excludes boundary points.
18. a) A **band** between two parallel lines (both boundaries **included**).
    b) ((0,0)): (0 \ge -1) true, (0 \le 2) true ⇒ **yes**.
19. Through ((-2,1)), ((2,-1)): slope (m=\dfrac{-1-1}{2-(-2)}=-\dfrac{2}{4}=-\tfrac{1}{2});
    Using ((2,-1)): (y=-\tfrac{1}{2}x + b\Rightarrow -1=-1+b\Rightarrow b=0).
    Below, not included ⇒ (\boxed{,y < -\tfrac{1}{2}x,}).
20. **No solutions.** Both have slope 1; (y>x+1) is above (y>x-5). You can’t be **above** the higher line and **below** the lower line simultaneously.
21. (\boxed{,y \ge -2,}). **Solid** horizontal line at (y=-2), shade **above**.
22. (\boxed{,x > -3,}). **Dashed** vertical line (x=-3); shade **right**.
23. Overlap = region between the two lines; ((3,0)): (0 \le 7) true, (0 \ge -5) true ⇒ **included**.
24. Intersections:

* (y=4) with (y=x-1) ⇒ (x=5) ⇒ ((5,4))
* (y=4) with (y=-x-1) ⇒ (-x-1=4\Rightarrow x=-5) ⇒ ((-5,4))
* (y=x-1) with (y=-x-1) ⇒ (x-1=-x-1\Rightarrow x=0,\ y=-1)
  Vertices: (\boxed{(-5,4),\ (5,4),\ (0,-1)}).

25. Edges:

* ((0,0))–((4,0)): (y=0 \Rightarrow \boxed{y \ge 0}) (interior above the (x)-axis)
* ((0,0))–((1,3)): (y=3x \Rightarrow \boxed{y \le 3x}) (check ((4,0)): (0 \le 12) true)
* ((4,0))–((1,3)): slope (-1), line (y=-x+4 \Rightarrow \boxed{y \le -x + 4}) (check interior ((\tfrac{5}{3},1)): (1 \le 2.\overline{3}) true)
  System: (\boxed{,y \ge 0,\ \ y \le 3x,\ \ y \le -x + 4,}).

:::
